opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it transfers surprisingly well, actually. The core recipe we developed for quadrupeds — training in massively parallel simulation on GPUs, using domain randomization for things like friction, mass, motor strength, and latency, and then designing a curriculum over terrains — that pipeline is pretty much agnostic to the morphology of the robot. You swap in a different URDF, adjust the reward terms, and a lot of the machinery just works.

That said, humanoids are harder in a few important ways. The first is stability. A quadruped standing still is statically stable; if the policy does something slightly wrong, the robot usually doesn't fall over. A humanoid is fundamentally unstable, with a small support polygon and a high center of mass, so the margin for error is much smaller. That makes the sim-to-real gap more punishing: small mismatches in actuator dynamics or contact modeling that a quadruped would shrug off can make a humanoid fall.

The second is the hardware itself. Humanoids often have more degrees of freedom, more complex transmissions, sometimes parallel linkages in the ankles or knees, and those are harder to model accurately in simulation. So you end up spending more effort on actuator modeling, things like actuator networks or careful system identification, to close that gap.

The third is the reward design and the motion style. With quadrupeds you can get away with fairly simple rewards, like tracking a velocity command, with some regularization, and the gaits that emerge look reasonable. With humanoids, people have strong expectations about what natural walking looks like, and pure reward shaping tends to give you strange, shuffly, or jittery behaviors. That's why you see a lot more use of motion capture data, imitation objectives, or adversarial motion priors in the humanoid space, to bias the policy toward human-like motion.

But overall I'd say the field moved from quadrupeds to humanoids so quickly precisely because the techniques transferred. The same simulators, the same PPO-based training setups, the same tricks for robustness. The difference is mostly in how much care you need to put into the details. And then on top of locomotion, humanoids open up whole-body control and loco-manipulation, which is where I think a lot of the really interesting open problems are now.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says the quadruped training pipeline and techniques transfer to humanoids, and that the field advanced quickly because those techniques transferred.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, a lot more transfers than people expected a few years ago. The core recipe we developed for quadrupeds — massively parallel simulation, a fairly simple PPO setup, domain randomization, a curriculum over terrain difficulty, and then sim-to-real with a good actuator model — that pipeline carries over almost unchanged. When we first moved to humanoids, we were a bit surprised that we didn't have to reinvent the method. The same training code, the same observation structure, roughly the same reward philosophy, and the policy learns to walk.

What doesn't transfer is the difficulty of the problem itself, and that shows up in a few places. The first is stability. A quadruped is statically stable for a large part of its gait, so the policy can make a lot of mistakes and the robot just stumbles and recovers. A humanoid is almost always in a dynamically unstable regime. The margin for error is much smaller, which means the sim-to-real gap matters more. Small discrepancies in the actuator response, in the contact model, in the mass distribution — things that a quadruped policy would absorb — can be the difference between walking and falling for a humanoid.

The second is reward design. With quadrupeds, you can get surprisingly far with a velocity-tracking reward and a handful of regularization terms, and the gait that emerges looks reasonable. With humanoids, if you just reward velocity tracking, the optimizer finds all sorts of strange solutions: shuffling gaits, bent knees, arms flailing, asymmetric steps. They're often perfectly valid from the reward's point of view, but they're not what you want on hardware, and they tend to be more fragile. So people end up putting a lot more structure in — reference motions, gait periodicity terms, symmetry constraints, or imitation of human motion capture. That's partly aesthetic, but it's also about robustness and about getting the policy into a region that the real robot can actually execute.

The third is the dimensionality and the role of the upper body. A quadruped's legs are basically the whole story. On a humanoid you have arms, a torso, often a lot of joints you don't strictly need for locomotion, and you have to decide what the policy controls and what it ignores. That interacts with the harder question, which is that nobody really wants a humanoid just to walk. The reason to build one is manipulation and whole-body tasks, and that's where I think the quadruped experience helps least, because the quadruped community mostly solved locomotion and stopped there.

So my overall view is: the learning techniques are shared, the engineering around them is shared, the simulators are shared. What changes is that the humanoid exposes the weaknesses of the approach more sharply. You need better system identification, more careful reward shaping or motion priors, and more thought about safety during deployment. I actually think that's healthy — the humanoid is forcing the field to be more rigorous about the parts of the pipeline we got away with being sloppy about on four legs.

r001.rationale: The response says the quadruped training pipeline carries over to humanoids and that the learning techniques are shared.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of the techniques transfer quite naturally. From the reinforcement-learning side, you still have a robot interacting with an environment, receiving observations, producing actions, and learning from a reward. That framework doesn’t fundamentally change when you go from four legs to two.

What changes is the difficulty of the control problem. A humanoid has fewer points of contact, and balance becomes more challenging. You also have more degrees of freedom, so you need to think carefully about the observations, the rewards, and how you structure the training. You shouldn’t expect to take a quadruped policy and just run it on a humanoid, but you can reuse much of the training approach.

And then there’s the transfer to hardware. Learning something in simulation is one part; making it robust to the actual robot’s dynamics, actuator limitations, and delays is another. So I see a lot of transferability in the methods, with substantial work still needed for the particular robot.

r001.rationale: The response says many reinforcement-learning techniques transfer naturally from quadrupeds to humanoids and that much of the training approach can be reused.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of the techniques transfer quite naturally. At the reinforcement-learning level, you still have a policy that takes observations from the robot and produces actions, and you train it in simulation. The tools we use for robustness—randomizing physical parameters, adding noise, and accounting for delays—are useful in both cases.

What changes is the difficulty of the control problem. A humanoid has more degrees of freedom, and balancing on two legs gives you less margin for error. You also have to think about what the upper body is doing and how that affects locomotion. So you can carry over much of the training framework, but you still need to adapt the observations, rewards, and training tasks to the particular robot.

The exciting part is that you don’t necessarily need a completely new algorithm for each morphology. A lot of the progress comes from setting up the learning problem well and giving the policy enough experience to discover a robust solution.

r001.rationale: The candidate says many reinforcement-learning techniques transfer naturally from quadrupeds to humanoids and identifies robustness tools useful in both.
